exercise_group.instructions: Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer. (If true, cite appropriate facts or theorems. If false, explain why or give a counterexample that shows why the statement is not true in every case.

statement.paragraph: (T/F) Every matrix is row equivalent to a unique matrix in echelon form.
(T/F) Any system of $n$ linear equations in $n$ variables has at most $n$ solutions.
(T/F) If a system of linear equations has two different solutions, it must have infinitely many solutions.
(T/F) If a system of linear equations has no free variables, then it has a unique solution.

(T/F) If an augmented matrix $\lbrack A\quad\mathbf{b}\rbrack$ is transformed into $\lbrack C\quad\mathbf{d}\rbrack$ by elementary row operations, then the equations $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ and $C\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{d}$ have exactly the same solution sets.
(T/F) If a system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has more than one solution, then so does the system $A\mathbf{x} = 0$.
(T/F) If $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix and the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is consistent for some $\mathbf{b}$, then the columns of $A$ span $\text{ℝ}^{m}$.
(T/F) If an augmented matrix $\lbrack A\quad\mathbf{b}\rbrack$ can be transformed by elementary row operations into reduced echelon form, then the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is consistent.
(T/F) If matrices $A$ and $B$ are row equivalent, they have the same reduced echelon form.
(T/F) The equation $A\mathbf{x} = 0$ has the trivial solution if and only if there are no free variables.
(T/F) If $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix and the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is consistent for every $\mathbf{b}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{m}$, then $A$ has $m$ pivot columns.
(T/F) If an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ has a pivot position in every row, then the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has a unique solution for each $\mathbf{b}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{m}$.
(T/F) If an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ has $n$ pivot positions, then the reduced echelon form of $A$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix.
(T/F) If $3 \times 3$ matrices $A$ and $B$ each have three pivot positions, then $A$ can be transformed into $B$ by elementary row operations.

(T/F) If $A$ is an $m \times n$ matrix, if the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has at least two different solutions, and if the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c}$ is consistent, then the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c}$ has many solutions.
(T/F) If $A$ and $B$ are row equivalent $m \times n$ matrices and if the columns of $A$ span $\text{ℝ}^{m}$, then so do the columns of $B$.

(T/F) If none of the vectors in the set $S = \{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{3}\}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ is a multiple of one of the other vectors, then $S$ is linearly independent.
(T/F) If $\{\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{w}\}$ is linearly independent, then $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$, and $\mathbf{w}$ are not in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$.
(T/F) In some cases, it is possible for four vectors to span $\text{ℝ}^{5}$.
(T/F) If $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are in $\text{ℝ}^{m}$, then $- \mathbf{u}$ is in $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\}$.
(T/F) If $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$, and $\mathbf{w}$ are nonzero vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$, then $\mathbf{w}$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$.
(T/F) If $\mathbf{w}$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, then $\mathbf{u}$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$.

(T/F) Suppose that $\mathbf{v}_{1}$, $\mathbf{v}_{2}$, and $\mathbf{v}_{3}$ are in $\text{ℝ}^{5}$, $\mathbf{v}_{2}$ is not a multiple of $\mathbf{v}_{1}$, and $\mathbf{v}_{3}$ is not a linear combination of $\mathbf{v}_{1}$ and $\mathbf{v}_{2}$. Then $\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent.
(T/F) A linear transformation is a function.
(T/F) If $A$ is a $6 \times 5$ matrix, the linear transformation $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ cannot map $\text{ℝ}^{5}$ onto $\text{ℝ}^{6}$.

Write the vector $\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 5 \\ 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack$ as the sum of two vectors, one on the line $\{(x\text{,~}y):y = 2x\}$ and one on the line $\{(x\text{,~}y):y = x/2\}$.

statement.paragraph: Construct a $2 \times 3$ matrix $A$, not in echelon form, such that the solution of $A\mathbf{x} = 0$ is a line in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$.
Construct a $2 \times 3$ matrix $A$, not in echelon form, such that the solution of $A\mathbf{x} = 0$ is a plane in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$.

Write the reduced echelon form of a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A$ such that the first two columns of $A$ are pivot columns and $A\,\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 2} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack\, = \,\,\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$.
In (a) and (b), suppose the vectors are linearly independent. What can you say about the numbers $a\text{,\,\,…\,\,,}\,f$? Justify your answers. [Hint:Use a theorem for (b).]
Use Theorem 7 in Section 1.7 to explain why the columns of the matrix $A$ are linearly independent.

Explain why a set $\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{3}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{4}\}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{5}$ must be linearly independent when $\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent and $\mathbf{v}_{4}$ is not in $\text{Span~}\left\{ \mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{3} \right\}$.

Suppose $\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\}$ is a linearly independent set in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Show that $\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{1} + \mathbf{v}_{2}\}$ is also linearly independent.

Suppose $\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{3}$ are distinct points on one line in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$. The line need not pass through the origin. Show that $\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly dependent.
Let $T:\text{ℝ}^{n}\rightarrow\text{ℝ}^{m}$ be a linear transformation, and suppose $T(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{v}$. Show that $T( - \mathbf{u}) = - \mathbf{v}$.

Let $T:\text{ℝ}^{3}\rightarrow\text{ℝ}^{3}$ be the linear transformation that reflects each vector through the plane $x_{2} = 0$. That is, $T(x_{1}\text{,~}x_{2}\text{,~}x_{3}) = (x_{1}\text{,} - x_{2}\text{,~}x_{3})$. Find the standard matrix of $T$.

Let $A$ be a $3 \times 3$ matrix with the property that the linear transformation $\mathbf{x}\mapsto A\mathbf{x}$ maps $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ onto $\text{ℝ}^{3}$. Explain why the transformation must be one-to-one.

A Givens rotation is a linear transformation from $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ to $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ used in computer programs to create a zero entry in a vector (usually a column of a matrix). The standard matrix of a Givens rotation in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ has the form
statement.math: $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} a & {- b} \\ b & a \end{array} \right\rbrack\text{,~}\qquad a^{2} + b^{2} = 1$$

A large apartment building is to be built using modular construction techniques. The arrangement of apartments on any particular floor is to be chosen from one of three basic floor plans. Plan A has $18$ apartments on one floor, including $3$ three-bedroom units, $7$ two-bedroom units, and $8$ one-bedroom units. Each floor of plan B includes $4$ three-bedroom units, $4$ two-bedroom units, and $8$ one-bedroom units. Each floor of plan C includes $5$ three-bedroom units, $3$ two-bedroom units, and $9$ one-bedroom units. Suppose the building contains a total of $x_{1}$ floors of plan A, $x_{2}$ floors of plan B, and $x_{3}$ floors of plan C.
